speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: We'll hear argument next in Case 24-889, Hikma Pharmaceuticals versus Amarin Pharma.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Mr. Klein.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Under Section 271(b) of the Patent Act, selling a product suited for both infringing and substantial non -infringing uses is lawful unless the seller actively induces the infringing use.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Congress later passed Hatch-Waxman Section viii to ensure that one infringing use will not foreclose selling a  generic drug for a second non-infringing use. So public statements entirely consistent with selling skinny-label generic drug products under Section viii cannot actively induce infringement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Under our approach and the one advanced by the United States, "actively induce infringement" when dealing with statements requires a clear message that necessarily promotes infringement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The Court applied this  standard in Grokster and more recently in Cox.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Active inducement cannot depend on whether doctors might read infringing instructions into product descriptions that, on their face, are entirely consistent with non-infringing use.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Amarin argues that generic drug companies must constantly discourage  infringement with disclaimers that are explicit.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: But that turns the statute on its head.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Agreeing with Amarin, the Federal Circuit basically swapped the statutory term "active" for its antonym, "passive."  And under  the decision below, patent lawsuits filed after skinny -label product launches will routinely survive a pleading challenge.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: This shuts the Section viii pathway down.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Generic companies won't choose that pathway if, at best, it means  paying millions in legal fees and, at worst, a massive damages award.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Reversal is needed to harmonize Section viii with Section 271(b) and to encourage legitimate competition that reduces drug prices.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: I welcome the Court's questions.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: Wouldn't it have been safe to just simply say that -- that the generic drug was -- was only approved for the SH indication and nothing more?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Your Honor, Hikma did say that when it launched its product in the November press release, and it did say that on the accused website.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: But the law does not  require that.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: In Grokster and Cox, the Court made clear that failure to take affirmative steps to prevent infringement is -- is not what the standard  --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: But what if you  -- what if Respondent had engaged in a certain degree of self-adulation and said that this is a great product for this, that, or the other, and you merely quoted it?  Wouldn't that almost be baiting people into inducement -- or inducing people into using the product more  broadly than the unpatented use?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The hypothetical is  -- is a little vague, but if -- if Hikma or a generic  were to send a clear message that --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: Well, not using your language but using their language.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: They have patented uses that they think are great, but you could  --why didn't you -- you simply quote them.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: Wouldn't that be a way to induce?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: If  --if Hikma quoted Amarin --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: Yeah.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: --with regard to its cardiovascular use  --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: Yeah.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: --that could plausibly state a claim if -- if it's a clear message that necessarily promotes infringement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The -- the Grokster Court addressed a similar type of situation when distinguishing  the Sony case and -- and  --and distinguished statements like "record favorite shows on your  Betamax" and said that does not encourage conduct that necessarily infringes, and, therefore, that's not actively induced infringement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And if you don't actively induce infringement, you fall under Section 271(c) --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: I  --I think what I'm asking you is, is the only way to actively induce infringement is overstating or your own statements sound as though the patented use is covered by your product, as opposed to simply  quoting the Respondent's website or statements about its product, which is patented?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: I  -- I'm not saying there is any kind of magic words standard.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And if  -- if the generic basically adopts by reference statements by the  -- the --the brand that would -- that would encourage the infringing  use, then that could plausibly state a claim.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: Do you need any of the special rules that you're claiming we have to announce to win this case?  Does this pass Twombly and Iqbal?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: It does, and -- and our --

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: It passes Twombly and Iqbal?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Our case, yeah.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: Yeah, meaning --

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Easily.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: -- the complaint here  --

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The complaint  --

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: -- is adequate under Twombly and Iqbal?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Oh, I'm sorry.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: I'm sorry. I thought you  --I -- I misunderstood the question.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The -- no, the --the complaint does not pass the standard for plausibility under Twombly and Iqbal.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Our argument --

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: That -- that  -- that's the point --

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Yes, yes.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: -- which is you're asking us to announce rules that  -- that -- almost impossible in this area because determining whether or not there's active inducement is always contextual.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: I think Grokster said that one of the factors it used was that the name that the  infringer was using was suggestive of the infringement.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: So that wasn't an express  statement of any way to infringe.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: It was a suggestion.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: But, in context with other things, it reached active inducement.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: I'm asking a very simple question. You don't need all of the things you've been  arguing about to win under Twombly and Iqbal, correct?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That is correct.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The statements here, as the government called them, were anodyne.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: They  -- they --they were unoffensive.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: They were totally consistent --

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: Now I do know that we make life hard because we say we're not  going to take on error correction, so you had to make up a rule of some sort, but it seems like everything you say, like somehow you need express statements as opposed to what we have said, you need active inducement.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: You want to change the words, but do we need to change any of our standards for you to win?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: No, Your Honor, because there are obvious alternative explanations in view of the anodyne statements.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Every single accused statement has an  --has an explanation that is entirely consistent with non-infringement.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: All right.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: Thank you, counsel.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: Can I ask you a similarly straightforward question?  With respect to Amarin's allegations concerning the  label, I had understood that by statute, generics have to have a label that essentially, in all relevant circumstances, mirrors the brand label, except for just admitting the patented indication.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: Is that correct?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That is correct.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: It's called the sameness requirement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That's by statute.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Now --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: So it's  -- so even if Amarin is right that it thinks that -- that Hikma could have or should have excluded a certain study or included the -- some other information, if those aren't on the original label, Hikma can't do that?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Hikma cannot change the label, but I want to be clear about something because Amarin supplied to the FDA the sections that Amarin thought pertained to its patent.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And then the way the FDA, the -- the skinny -label process works is the FDA compares what Amarin says is patented in the label to the proposed skinny label, and it's a ministerial role.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: If  -- if the generic carved out everything that the brand said is patented, then the skinny label can be approved.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And the generic can't add new disclaimers or -- or new language.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: Or anything else. And it can't be accused of inducing infringement by refusing to put things on the label that the brand didn't have, right?

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That's true because of the statutory scheme.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That's true because Grokster  and Cox says there's -- they're --the statute doesn't require active discouragement of  infringement and for all of those reasons.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: I -- I also want to point out how Grokster warned against trenching on regular commerce, and that is exactly the situation  here because the regular commerce we're talking about here is commerce that's encouraged by Congress.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: It's -- it's Section viii skinny -label products. And as a practical matter, under the decision below, you can get FDA approval of your skinny product label, but as soon as you put that product into commerce and you say anything about that product, anything, you call  it a generic version, even if you have disclaimers, you can be sued.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And that lawsuit will survive a pleading challenge.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And that sends a  --a terrible message to the generic industry. Hatch-Waxman was designed to resolve patent disputes before a product launch for the  -- for the reason that it's the  --it's an economic reason.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Once a generic launches its product, its profits will be much, much lower than the brand's profits.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And so, if the generic gets  hit for a lost profits damages award, it's devastating.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: This happened in the GSK case with Teva, and Teva got hit for hundreds of millions of dollars that dwarfed its actual profits.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And that is what the decision below is encouraging, and that's why we -- we are urging the Court to reverse.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Anything else? Anything else?  No? Thank you, counsel. Mr. Stewart.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  I'd like to begin with two very brief observations.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The first point is that although  the Federal Circuit appropriately said that the label itself was not sufficient to get Amarin past 12(b)(6) in this case, we think the court of appeals erred in giving any weight at all to the label.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The contents of a Hatch-Waxman skinny label are largely dictated by federal law, and  to treat the generic manufacturers' compliance with those requirements as any evidence of intentional inducement to infringe would be wrong.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The second thing is, when Respondents explain in their brief why they sued Hikma but haven't sued any of the other generic manufacturers of icosapent ethyl, their explanation is all of those other manufacturers  included in press releases express disclaimers to the effect that their product is not authorized for use to treat the CV indication.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: But it's a bedrock principle of inducement law that active inducement to infringe is required. The question is not whether the defendant has adequately warned people away from infringement.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I welcome the Court's questions.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: What would Respondent have to have alleged to survive a motion to dismiss?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I think they would have had to --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: In your world, not the Fed Circuit's world.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: In -- in our world, the Respondent would have had to  --to identify statements or actions that had the clear purpose of induce  -- of causing others to infringe as something that the -- the brand wanted to bring about.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The Court in Grokster said it was with reference to copyright, but it was drawing on copyright  --on patent law principles. The Court said one who distributes a device with the object of promoting its use to infringe copyright, as shown by clear expression or other affirmative steps taken to foster infringement, is liable for the resulting acts of infringement by third parties.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And so they would have needed to  point to statements or actions that clearly revealed a purpose to induce infringement.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: What role  -- what impact is it that occurs in states that  encourage the use of the generics for the patented use?  What does that have on the  problem that the Respondent is having?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, I -- I think one of the principles that emerges from this Court's cases and from Cox most recently --

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: No, I don't mean on this.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: I mean with the problems of the -- of the unpatented, the generic being used for uses  that are still patented by Respondent.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, the preliminary point I would make is the perceived difficulty  or the actual difficulty of going after the direct infringer or getting the direct infringement to start -- to -- to stop is not a justification for watering down inducement principles.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Now there are other things that Respondents could try to do and some of them they have tried to do.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: They sued Health Net in this case, and they separately alleged that the health insurer, through its reimbursement  policies, was encouraging pharmacies to fill the drug fully.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: But aren't some states doing that too?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, states certainly have these generic substitution laws.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And I'm  not sure to what extent states are regulating the health insurers, but, certainly, Amarin and  similarly situated companies could urge state legislatures to take measures to prevent this from happening.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The other thing they could do, I understand they don't want to sue the doctors,  but they could attempt informational campaigns to doctors and tell the doctors our product is the only one that is authorized to be used for the CV indication.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It would be infringement of  patent to administer icosapent ethyl for the purpose of reducing cardiovascular risk. And the doctor really is in the best position of any other -- any single actor to  say for what purpose am I prescribing the drug and at least in theory could figure out is there a patent on one method of use and adjust prescribing practices accordingly.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: I understood that the test that you articulated is that the  -- what was required is that the generic person clearly reveal a purpose of infringement, is that --

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Act  -- acts or messages that reveal a clear intent to encourage infringement.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: That's a pretty broad safe harbor.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: I mean, you really  just have to have, you know, a seminar on your first day of work and say whatever you do, don't -- don't do that.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: It's pretty easy  -- it  -- it's a pretty high threshold -- or low threshold.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I -- I mean, it is supposed to be a -- a difficult standard for the pleader to satisfy, but I think that's for design.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: That is, the Court has said in various contexts that when a product is capable of both infringing and non-infringing use --uses, it's important that a patent on one method of use not become a de facto monopoly on the product as a whole.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And so it's supposed to be feasible for people in Hikma's position to market their product for the unpatented use without running  afoul of liability for third parties who choose to use the product in infringing ways.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Unless  they have affirmatively encouraged that to be done, the mere knowledge that it will be done  or the expectation that some people will infringe is not enough.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: And the risk of liability and what it could do to a generic, I would think, would be pretty significant.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It's very substantial in part because the generic is charging a lot -- typically, a lot less for the drug than the brand-name manufacturer is.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And so, if the generic has to pay lost profits to the -- the brand name, the profits that the brand name  would have earned on a particular volume of sales would -- would be much more than the generic has actually earned.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: And the product is substantially similar.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: I mean, that's why it's a generic.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: So, in other words, there's no  defense that, well, we really have a different product here.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: We  -- it's --it's the generic of the drug, and so, if they're also liable absent active inducement for people taking their generic and using it in an infringing  way, you would think that could happen a fair  amount, and it would really be a risk to the bottom line of this generic company.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Yes.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, there -- there is an intimation -- more than an intimation in the Respondents' brief that Hikma was doing something wrong by describing its drug in press releases as a generic version or a generic equivalent of Vascepa.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: But, in fact, that's a normal thing to say.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It really refers to two different things. One of them is, under the abbreviated new drug application process, the generic comes on the  market not by conducting independent studies of safety and efficacy but by showing that it is equivalent to a drug that's already been found safe and efficacious.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And so, when Hikma says we're the generic version of Vascepa, they just mean Vascepa is what's called the reference listed drug.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It is the drug as to which we  established equivalence in order to get approval.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The second thing is that the patents in these cases refer to methods of reducing cardiovascular -- risk of cardiovascular events or cardiovascular death, and the method they describe is the use of what the patent refers to as ethyl icosapent in various ways, a series  of steps with certain types of patients.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And everybody agrees, if Hikma's drug is used to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death or events through the performance of those steps, infringement will occur.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The  reason that's so is that Hikma's drug is ethyl icosapent.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It's the same stuff.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And it's the same stuff for infringement purposes, but it's  also the same stuff for describing the product.

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: Can you explain the United States' concerns about the broader market implications of the decision?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, I think we would divide the -- the --what the Federal Circuit relied on into three categories.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The one we were most concerned with was the skinny label because all of the things that Amarin is complaining about are things that were on the brand name's label, and the rule is the generic is supposed to use the same label as the brand unless there's a good patent-specific reason to take things off.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And so the Federal Circuit, I think, thought it was being limited by saying the label by itself is not enough to get past  12(b)(6), but the flavor of its opinion was this is almost enough, and if you have some pretty ethereal stuff at the  --in addition, that will be enough to get you over the hump. And we think it shouldn't have attached any weight to the label.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Hikma just did what it was supposed to do.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And then the second thing is the description of the  --Hikma's generic product as the generic version --

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: I understand that, but the interest -- the implications of the decision in the marketplace at large, I understood -- do you want to speak to that or  not speak to that?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Yes.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, I -- I think the FDA's view is it is too soon to tell  exactly what the effects of the Federal Circuit's decision would be on the willingness of other generic manufacturers to enter the marketplace.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And, in part, I assume that  generics are waiting on this Court's decision in this case, but we certainly think that if the Federal Circuit's analysis were affirmed, that it would create a substantial disincentive to entering the generic market.

speaker: Samuel A. Alito, Jr.
text: What if --

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: Your point  --no, go ahead.

speaker: Samuel A. Alito, Jr.
text: What if Hikma -- Hikma had  -- had not just said its drug is generic Vascepa but went on to say that Vascepa is approved to treat cardiovascular risks?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I think if it had said those two things in the  --in the same breath that you would have a pretty strong case of active inducement, that it would not take much work to connect the dots that this is something Vascepa has been approved for and ours is the same stuff.

speaker: Samuel A. Alito, Jr.
text: What if it had said studies have shown that icosapent ethyl, the active ingredient in our drug, reduces cardiovascular risks?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I think that would be problematic as -- as well, although probably closer to the line, but one thing I would say about the label is, when Hikma prepared its skinny label in conformity with the rules, kind of the most obvious thing it took off of Amarin's label was the indication at the beginning.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: But a second thing that it took off of Amarin's label was, in the clinical studies section of Amarin's label, Amarin summarized the results of what they call the REDUCE-IT study, which was designed to test the efficacy of the product for reducing cardiovascular risks, and the study concluded that Vascepa was efficacious for this purpose.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And  --

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: I  -- I see your red light is on.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Okay.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Justice Thomas?

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: No.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor?

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: I asked the same question of you that I asked of Petitioners' counsel.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: Do we need your new definition that  you gave the Chief or saying again that following the label alone, exactly what the Federal Circuit said, is not enough?  Do we  need any special rules --

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I don't  --

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: -- for Petitioner to win?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I -- I don't think you need special rules.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I  -- you are interpreting Section 271(b), which is not specific to Hatch-Waxman.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It's just the general inducement provision.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And we think application of the  general rules is sufficient.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: Is enough?  Okay.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Yes.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: And then, finally, there's a whole lot of discussion about congressional policy, both in your brief and in Petitioners' brief, that they wanted to encourage this, and we should rule that what active infringement means in patent law is very narrow because of that.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: I always have problems when we use policy reasons to set a standard.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Right.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: That's not our job.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: If they're infringing a patent, they're infringing a patent.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: If they're not infringing a patent, they're not.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: But why should we change our rules, narrow them or expand them  --

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I don't  --

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: -- to avoid either result?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I -- I basically agree. I don't think it's a main -- matter of changing the rules.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: We have described the Hatch-Waxman scheme at some length because it's pretty complicated.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: But, in the end, Hatch-Waxman embodies the same basic principles as the Patent Act generally; namely, if you sell  something that can be used either in an infringing or a non-infringing way, then you still won't be held liable for others'  infringement unless you've actively encouraged them to infringe.

speaker: Sonia Sotomayor
text: That's the bottom line, correct?  Thank you.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Justice Kagan?

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: Mr. Stewart, your point about not looking to the skinny label in  a suit like this, I guess the reasonableness of that depends on how much patent review the FDA  is doing when it approves the skinny label.

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: So what's the answer to that question?

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I mean, I think the -- the Court discussed this in Caraco.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The FDA has disclaimed patent expertise, and so it  doesn't purport to read patents and determine what conduct would infringe them.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: But Respondents suggest that the result is we take the generics' word for what is and isn't infringing.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And I think that that's not correct.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: As the Court explained in Caraco, the brand-name manufacturer will provide for the Orange Book what's called a use code, which will describe what it believes its patents cover, and the FDA considers itself bound by the use code.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And so, if the brand name is saying this wide range of uses would be patented, the FDA won't look behind that.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: There is a counterclaim mechanism by which the  -- the generic can obtain judicial review of that determination  --of the brand's behavior in a suit between the two private parties.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: But the  -- kind of the bottom line is, here, there was really no dispute about what  was patented.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: If there had been a dispute, FDA would have deferred to the brand's own  description of what its patent covered, and then the question would just be, has the generic carved out enough of the label to  excise references to the patented use?  And what I was saying before about the clinical studies, although Amarin's label had a description of the REDUCE-IT study that was about efficacy of the drug for treating cardiovascular -- or preventing cardiovascular events, Hikma omitted that from its own label. So it didn't just omit the indication.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: It  omitted another part of the label that referred to the efficacy of the drug for that purpose because the purpose was still patented.

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: Thank you.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Justice Gorsuch, anything further?  Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson?

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: Can I just ask you, what  --what is the relevance of the state laws that you cite permitting or requiring substitution of generics for brand-name drugs in this context?  I would think those would be relevant to an Amarin lawsuit maybe against a third party, but I don't know why they matter here.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: I -- I mean, I think the Court can decide the case without referring to them.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The -- we had two basic reasons for including some discussion.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: The  --the first was we didn't want the Court to decide the case based on a misimpression of the facts or the way the world works.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And I think portions of the court of appeals opinion are written as though, in -- in each case, the doctor who's writing the prescription determines which version of the drug will be dispensed and that will carry the day.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And we wanted to explain, in the real world, it's more complicated than that.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: And -- and kind of conceivably in some future case, that could matter given the way it was pleaded because you'd have to show, in light of these laws, how is it plausible that what we said  would cause somebody to infringe.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: I see.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Thank you, counsel.

speaker: Malcolm L. Stewart
text: Thank you.

speaker: John G. Roberts, Jr.
text: Mr. Huston.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  The implications of this Court's ruling in this case will go far beyond the pharmaceutical industry.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: This is not really a Hatch-Waxman case at all.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It's not really a skinny -label case. Hikma got the full benefit of the Hatch-Waxman compromise when it was permitted to sell its product for FDA -- with an FDA approved skinny label as a treatment for severe hypertriglyceridemia.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: But, in exchange, Hikma  was required to promise not to promote its product for any still patented use of Amarin's branded drug.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That limitation on generic marketing of their products is absolutely vital.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It is the only thing that makes it economically  rational for a branded company like Amarin to spend the $300 million that Amarin spent in the REDUCE -IT trial to discover that an existing drug, Vascepa, actually had life-changing implications to treat cardiovascular risk.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And  that rule of induced infringement liability is not unique to pharmaceuticals.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: This Court's interpretation in this case will be of Section 271(b) of the Patent Act.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That is the statute that protects all  patented innovations in this country of whatever kind.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The standard for induced infringement liability is settled.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: In most cases, the key dispute is going to be whether the defendant had the requisite intent to infringe.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: But Hikma has not contested its intent as this case comes to the Court because the case is at the pleading stage.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Nor has Hikma disputed that there was substantial direct infringement of Amarin's patents using Hikma's product.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So the only  element that's in dispute here today is whether it is plausible that Hikma took active steps to  encourage that infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It is plausible.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: There are seven other generic manufacturers of icosapent ethyl on the market, but Hikma alone was the one who described its product as AB rated for "hypertriglyceridemia," even though that product is not approved for that distinct medical condition.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Hikma alone repeatedly used Amarin's brand name, Vascepa, just at the moment when  that name was synonymous in the market with treating cardiovascular risk.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Those statements  and more by Hikma that other generics did not use state a plausible claim.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I welcome the Court's questions.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: Was there anything inaccurate about that statement?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Yes, there absolutely was, Your Honor.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And I want to just say for -- it was inaccurate.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I also don't think, frankly, it matters whether it was inaccurate. A statement can be absolutely true.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Imagine a statement that Hikma said you can use and should use our product to accomplish exactly  the same medical purposes as Vascepa, including cardiovascular risk, the kind of example that I  think Justice Alito gave to my friend, Mr. Stewart.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And I heard Mr. Stewart say that would state a claim for induce  --a strong claim for induced agreement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I agree with that.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So truth is not a defense to liability in an induced infringement situation.

speaker: Clarence Thomas
text: So what if they simply quote you?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think they can't  -- they cannot do that, Your Honor, because the whole point of the compromise is that Hikma is allowed to market its product but only for the unpatented use, only as a treatment for severe hypertriglyceridemia. If Hikma comes on and quotes Amarin's marketing of its product to treat for the patented purpose, that's the most classic case of induced infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That's like the  literal textbook definition of induced infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I -- I also do think it's important to say, though, that the -- the key statement on which we rely here, the statement on Hikma's  website where it described what its drug is for, was not accurate.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Hikma said its product was for treating hypertriglyceridemia.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That's misleading, if not false, because Hikma's  product was approved by FDA only to treat severe hypertriglyceridemia, and that's a  distinct medical condition that presents distinct medical risks.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Well, if that's your best piece, and I think it probably is, that website, what do you do with -- there was a further disclaimer on the website saying that the product was  -- Hikma's generic version is indicated for fewer than all approved indications of the reference listed drug?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Sure, Your Honor.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So two points about that disclaimer, which is at JA 195.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: First, as you can see even on the blown-up version in the Joint Appendix, it really appears in quite tiny print, but even if the -- even if somebody read it, even if  they saw the disclaimer, just as Your Honor read, all it says is Hikma's product is approved for fewer than all uses of Vascepa.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It doesn't disclaim that Hikma's product can and should be used to treat the most famous use of Vascepa, the billion -dollar use, which is saving patients' lives by treating cardiovascular risk.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So there's nothing  -- the disclaimer is, I think, at best, carefully worded, it's  sort of written by a clever lawyer to try to minimize Hikma's liability while still sending the fundamental message that is coming across by all the collection of Hikma's statements that says doctors can and should prescribe  Hikma's product anytime they would prescribe Vascepa, including to treat cardiovascular risk, in a way that infringes Amarin's patents.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So I --

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: Oh, go ahead.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I just think having rang the bell, Your Honor, having repeated  --when Hikma has come on to the market repeatedly and  said we are generic Vascepa, generic Vascepa, generic Vascepa, a billion dollars in sales, our product is for hypertriglyceridemia, having made all of those offensive statements that are calculated that have the intent to induce  infringing sales, that tiny little sort of cleverly worded disclaimer I don't think is sufficient to pull that back.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: Mr. Huston, I just wondered, if you -- you started in your opening  talking about the impact of this case that would be more broad, that it would extend beyond just the pharmaceutical industry.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: It seems to me this is a pretty fact-bound case about the plausibility standard.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: I don't know that we have to -- to reach any kind of greater issue.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: So do you see  the case that way?  Is this just kind of applying Twiqbal to this particular complaint?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I do see the case that way, Your Honor.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: We  --we -- that's what we argued in our brief in opposition. And I think that it's not this Court's typical practice to grant a case that asks merely whether the facts as pleaded under the  -- you know, a settled legal standard states a claim.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: All that said, you know, of course, we  -- we -- we  --we continue to think, and I  -- I do want to think -- I do think it's very important to say, it is important, as I think the  --was the premise of Justice Sotomayor's questions, that the Court not adopt a new  induced infringement standard with words like express promotion is required.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I -- I -- I can't -- I just can't understate the extent to which that would be a transformation of the scope of patent law.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So,  if the Court is going to simply apply Twombly and Iqbal to the facts of this case, and I -- I do think that's the right approach to the case, then I continue to think that the key question in the case is in  --in --as in most cases of induced infringement, what was the message that the doctors who read these Hikma statements took away?  And that's typically a fact question.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: I -- I agree that's the key question, it is a fact question, and, you know, Justice Alito observed the other day, I'm not sure why this case is here except four of my colleagues wanted it to be.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: But, if it is a fact-bound question, what I'm asking is, if the case is as you just described it, what's the broader impact?  You know, in  --in your  -- are you talking about broader impact solely if we reached some new rule?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Yeah.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: No, I  --I'm totally  --

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: Okay.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Let me -- I appreciate the opportunity to clarify.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: If the Court says that even though this case is at the pleading stage, even though it's only a plausibility pleading standard, these allegations of intentional -- intentional statements by Hikma where intent is undisputed,  that that doesn't even state a claim for relief, I do think that's going to have serious implications.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It's going to make it much, much  harder to plead induced patent infringement. And I think that's going to have implications both in the patent space more generally but even in the pharmaceutical space  because, as I mentioned, if -- if -- if a -- if a branded drug like Amarin cannot get any kind of protection for a new -- this newly discovered use of its existing drug, it would  just be economically irrational to make that kind of investment that discovers a lifesaving cure.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And I think that's what we are really fighting for in this case, is the opportunity to say:  We spent five years, we spent $300  million, and we discovered something that is literally saving people's lives.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Hikma wants  to come and, having spent no money basically at all, try to capture all of those gains.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The patent law doesn't allow them to do that.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: They are allowed to sell their product for the unpatented use.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: But, when we have discovered this game-changing "new use," Hikma can't come in and try to capture those -- those -- those sales.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That's what it did with its repeated statements by calling itself generic Vascepa over and over again by mis --

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: Would  -- would --

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: What --

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: -- would you contest, Mr. Huston, that these press releases were really issued for investors, that they had nothing to do with  -- this was not the way the company marketed itself to doctors?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I  --I would contest that, Your Honor, especially because we're at  the pleading stage, where all inferences that  are fair have to be taken in our favor.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think Hikma's claim that these were directed at investors is really just grounded in the fact that there's a "Contact Us" section of the press release that allows you to get in touch with the investor relations team, in  addition to other kinds of, you know, phone numbers provided.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So they're not consciously  directed at investors, not expressly directed at investors.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And I think two other points about that.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: First, Hikma spread these messages far and wide.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It wanted  --

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: I mean, is there any evidence at all that Hikma directed these to -- to the medical community, that Hikma gave these press releases to doctors?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So I think the answer is yes in the sense that these  -- this is advertising, Your Honor, which is, as Grokster said, a classic form of induced infringement since common law.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Hikma, the -- our allegations are  --we don't have evidence; we're at the pleading stage  -- but the allegations we have are that Hikma took these press releases and intentionally attempted to  make them get distributed as far and widely as possible.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It did want doctors to see these things.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And evidence has come in in other cases where doctors have testified that they do pay attention to press releases and that they do pay attention to the announcements of when generics are coming online, and those kinds of announcements do affect doctors' prescription decisions.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So that's all evidence that, you know, we're going to put on -- you know, that -- those -- we're going to use the Federal Circuit's established standards for pleading induced  -- or for proving induced infringement claims.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It only has to be plausible at this stage.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And I don't think it's a fair inference  --I don't think you can say the only fair inference from Hikma's statements is that they were directed solely at investors and were  not going to reach doctors.

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: But I guess, to your initial statement when you started out  saying this is not a Hatch-Waxman case at all, I think you said that, and to why this case is here, because I'm glad it's here, the federal  --Congressman Waxman filed an amicus brief.

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: And I don't want to put too much faith in a former Congressman's brief about his own statute, but it says, "the Federal Circuit's  decision threatens to decimate the compromise at the heart of the Hatch-Waxman Act, which, in turn, threatens to undermine the generic  pharmaceutical industry if this kind of complaint's good enough."  And it points out, you know, "generics have saved 3.4 trillion over the past 10 years, but the Federal Circuit's decision here leaves generic drug companies in the dark about what might expose them to liability."  All of which is to say I think the question is, you know, if this is good enough, then that's going to have some serious implications market-wide.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So, Justice Kavanaugh, maybe two or maybe three points if I might in response to that.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: First, when we say "if it's good enough," all we mean is good enough to get out of the starting gate, to get into discovery, where we're going to have the opportunity  -- we're going to be held to the burden to prove everything that we allege.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That's the first point.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The second point about Hatch-Waxman is that the reason it's named Hatch-Waxman, of course, is that it was a fundamental  compromise, and on the other side of that compromise was about protecting the need to  encourage branded drugs to take existing products and invest massive resources to discover how those drugs can be used for new cures.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The dark green briefs are replete with examples of situations where that has happened. It can only happen, it's only economically rational to occur, if they can get patent protection for that subsequent use.

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: Yeah.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And then I think the last  --

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: I don't dispute that there's a compromise.

speaker: Brett M. Kavanaugh
text: I was just making  the point that, you know, I take it seriously  when someone says this is upsetting the compromise.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Well, I think the -- the  -- the last reason why the Court can have confidence that that is not going to come to pass, Your Honor, is the example of the many other generics who sell the very same product  that Hikma does, and we haven't sued any of them.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And you can look at what they say on their press release to know that generics have a ready roadmap to avoid induced infringement liability.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: All they have to do is accurately describe the limited purpose for which their drug is approved. So, for example, Camber, one of the other generic manufacturers, it says, "Camber's press release is indicated as an adjunct to  diet to reduce triglyceride levels in adult patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia."  It  doesn't talk about generic Vascepa.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It doesn't talk about the volume of sales of Vascepa and  say this is a billion-dollar revolutionary drug.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It doesn't say that it is in a  therapeutic category of hypertriglyceridemia. And, again, that's a different medical condition.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So Camber, Zydus, Dr. Ready's, they all  -- none of them do the things that Hikma did.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: Well, counsel  --

speaker: Samuel A. Alito, Jr.
text: Are you just saying  --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: -- can I --

speaker: Samuel A. Alito, Jr.
text: -- just -- are you just saying generic Vascepa would be enough?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I do not think, Your Honor, that merely saying one time generic  Vascepa is enough to state a claim for liability.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And that's not our allegation.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Our allegation is that Hikma said it over and over  and over again and that they did it at just the key moment where there was a market -- a market -- key market association between  Vascepa and treating cardiovascular risk.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That was the context.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Grokster says, of course, that induced infringement is a context-dependent analysis.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That was the context into which Hikma launched these statements over and over and over again.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: But I take the point.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I'm certainly not here to say that a company that one time says generic Vascepa is going to be held liable.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: As the Federal Circuit held, Hikma did much, much more.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It made statements that no other generic manufacturer --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: But, counsel, I guess it  -- it seems to me you -- you do emphasize that we're talking about plausibility and this is early in the case and we're at the motion -to-dismiss stage.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: But that does highlight what has to be plausible, what is the focus of this.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: And the government here, the SG, says what we're looking for is an intent on the part  of this manufacturer to be inducing people or to have doctors be using this drug for the patented purpose.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: Your standard, as far as I can tell, is more just what message would the doctors have taken away from the marketing materials. And, as Justice Kagan pointed out, at least  some of these marketing materials, I think, were directed to investors.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: So the  --if the intention of the generic is to mention Vascepa and the size of  the market, et cetera, et cetera, for the purpose of getting investment, not for the  purpose of inducing doctor infringement, what do we do with that in terms of understanding whether active inducement liability lies?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: A couple points about that, Justice Jackson.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think the first is  that, of course, at this stage of the case, your own  --you can't just take Hikma's assertion that, oh, we put out that press release for the purpose of talking to our investors.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: No, but it's your burden if we are supposed to be looking for intent.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: And I guess that's why I think we do have to kind of focus on what the legal standard is here.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: If  -- if --if we are looking for intent to induce infringement, then  I would think it's your burden to actually have statements and evidence that go to that.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: And if we look at those statements and we say, yes, we see them, but, really, those statements that you point to are indicative of  an intent to encourage investors, then why have you stated enough of a claim in this circumstance?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I understand the question, Your Honor, but I  -- I --I want to stress the Federal Circuit found that it was undisputed -- that's their word -- that in -- Hikma did not contest the requisite intent. That's at Pet. App. 15a.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Hikma's motion to dismiss in this case did not say, unlike most other skinny-label cases where intent, along the lines of Your  Honor's question, would very much be the focus and where I'm sure Hikma at trial will attempt to  -- to prove exactly the kinds of things that Your Honor --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: But is -- is the Federal Circuit right about that?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Yes --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: I don't know that we can disaggregate.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: I mean, they've  -- they -- they might have  -- Hikma might have said, we're not really focused on our intent to induce  something or our intent to have people buy more of this product.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: But, if the active inducement element of this is what we're all focused on and active  inducement requires an intent to induce doctors  to use this product, then I don't know that their concession about intent really covers this particular circumstance.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So, Your Honor, I mean, the Court has always talked about those as distinct elements of induced infringement. There are three elements.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: There has to be  direct infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Somebody has to do the infringing.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And then the inducer has to both have the intent that that happen and take active steps.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: I understand, but the United States today said the active inducement -- active steps prong of this is statements and acts that are  --that demonstrate an intent to induce the doctors.

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: So they brought intent into the very element we're talking about here.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: There's no way to reconcile that conception of the -- of the standard with this Court's case after case after case --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: So they're wrong about that?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: They're wrong  --

speaker: Ketanji Brown Jackson
text: All right.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: They're just distinct elements  --

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Well, how  --

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: --and the intent element isn't part of this case at this stage.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: I -- I'm sorry to interrupt.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Go ahead and finish.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I'm just  -- I just want to say that, I mean, the Court has always talked about them as distinct elements.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The Federal Circuit found that Hikma had not contested the intent element.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think -- actually, I thought it was common ground between all of the parties that we're only here talking about what constitutes active steps. These are active steps in the sense that Hikma put out statements.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And then I think the only question we're left with is the one Justice Barrett  flagged, which is how is a listener going to understand those statements?  That's a fact question that's typically not suitable for resolution on summary judgment.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That's the  crux of our case.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Justice?  I'm sorry.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: I'm not even sure I want to ask my question anymore, Mr. Huston.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: (Laughter.)

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Let me come at it this way.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: I understand your  --your -- your point about this case being a little different,  but, you know, Twombly/Iqbal talking about whether you have an antitrust conspiracy versus maybe what is entirely rational independent conduct, right?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Yes.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: The Baby Bells, right?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Yes.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Are not to compete in one another's territory.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Yes.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: It seems like a whole different world.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: At any rate, there, the question was, hey, everybody knows that they're not going  into each other's territory, but it could be explained by two possible intents, and it was the burden of the plaintiff to rule out, plausibly rule out, the non-problematic intent. And I  --I think what Justice Jackson is getting at is, why isn't this case just like that?  Why isn't that the question?  I understand your point that, well, they didn't  contest it, but it is your burden on -- on a motion -to-dismiss stage to -- to rule out that lawful intent, hey, this is puffery for investors, and this can be plausibly explained by  -- by that rather than infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think I would say two things, Your Honor.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The first is that it  -- it's  --it's very hard for me sitting here in the Supreme Court of the United States to put myself in what arguments we would have made if Hikma in a motion to dismiss had said we want to contest our unlawful intent the same way the defendant in Twombly contested its intent.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: You're absolutely right.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Twombly was an intent case.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That was where all the action in the case was.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Did the defendants have an unlawful intent?  Hikma did not contest its unlawful intent at this stage.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Okay.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: I got you.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So I just think it's a different  --but, I mean, the other  -- the other point I would make is, though -- even that kind of intuition, even a -- if you -- if you think, okay, there's a -- there's an  alternative explanation for the press releases, which is what  --that they were aimed at investors, that cannot explain Hikma's website, where it's described its  --it describes its product as a treatment for hypertriglyceridemia, the infringing use,  instead of, as all the other generic companies do, as a treatment --

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: Got you.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: --for severe hypertriglyceridemia use.

speaker: Neil Gorsuch
text: I got you.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So here again, I think you're -- you can't -- even that conception of the case cannot carve out all of the allegations we have made, all of which add up  together to support Hikma's unlawful intent and their active steps that have the effect of inducing infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And that is  fundamentally what we're going to be held to the burden to prove, as in all other cases of induced infringement.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: We're going to show that the infringing sales of our product happened faster and to a greater degree than would have occurred had Hikma not made these statements. And so, again, I -- I understand the Court's concern about the idea that, you know, and I think my friends have attempted to say this is going to devastate the generics market.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Nobody wants to devastate the generics market.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: But  it's just factually not true.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And the surest reason you can know it's not true is because there's seven other generics in this market selling this product who know how to market their product lawfully. And all that Hikma needed to do was follow that path and they wouldn't be here, just like the other generics aren't here.

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: Mr. Huston, my sense of your papers in this Court as compared maybe to your papers below is that you've really dialed down your reliance on the skinny label.

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: So could you tell me why that is if I'm right about that, and -- and more to the  point maybe, what is your view of the relevance of the skinny label?  Would you go -- would you accept Mr. Stewart's proposition that that label has no relevance?  And, if not, why not?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Sure.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So, Justice Kagan, I would not accept Mr. Stewart's proposition that that has no relevance, and I think the -- I think the reason for that is that this Court is not accustomed in pleading cases and in Section 271(b) cases to saying there's a  category of evidence that's sort of fundamentally off the table.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That to me sounds  like the creation of a safe harbor, and I think that's a legislative task fundamentally.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Now, to be sure, Hikma has  -- you know, I  -- I don't think Hikma could be held liable -- or, you know, I -- I -- I -- I think that there is a protection in the statute in Hatch-Waxman for -- for Hikma to prepare a skinny label.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That's why, as the Federal Circuit said, the skinny label is not the heart of our  case by any means.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It is one piece of evidence.

speaker: Elena Kagan
text: Well, why should it be one piece of evidence?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Sure.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Because, again, I don't think that the Court has generally said there's sort of evidence that's off the table. But the way I think about the label in this case, because keep in mind the label comes factually later in time.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: So it's really at the moment that Vascepa is all -- getting all of this amazing press attention that doctors are prescribing it en masse to -- for -- to  --for the first time really effectively treat patients with severe cardiovascular risk.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It's into that market  that Hikma launches all of its offensive statements about generic Vascepa, billion dollars in sales, hypertriglyceridemia and the like.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Then it comes out with its label.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And the way I think about the label is the label  was an opportunity for Hikma to try to -- to sort of mitigate the damage from its unlawful statements and it didn't take it.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And in that sense, I think the Hikma  --the Hikma label maybe -- you know, probably, arguably, exacerbated our harm.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: But that's the way I think about the label.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It's  --it is definitely not the  -- the key contention that we rely on because, again, it's not the thing that distinguishes Hikma from all the other generic manufacturers.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: They were  -- it was -- those generics made all of these statements that Hikma did not make, and I think that's why they're here -- that's why they're not here and Hikma is.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: The label just was an opportunity missed by Hikma  to try to control the extent of the infringement after they had already rang the bell.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think I just want to spend one moment if I might talking about where the Court would go from here if it found that this is a Twombly/Iqbal case and that the allegations in the current complaint did not suffice to state  a claim for relief.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: I think, as we described in our brief, the Court's far and away most common practice in that situation would be to vacate the Federal Circuit's opinion and remand.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: It would  not be to enter the form of judgment in this Court that Hikma requests, which would be to  sort of declare the case over.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: And I think that disposition, again, I  -- you know, obviously, we  --we hope that you will agree that the  -- the -- the -- the complaint here does state a claim, but in the event the Court didn't, it would be especially  important for the Court to allow the case to proceed back on remand because, since the Federal Circuit remanded the case and since Hikma did not stay the mandate, extensive discovery has occurred.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Millions of documents  have been exchanged, 12 depositions have -- have  --have come -- have been taken, and that has revealed substantial new evidence of Hikma's intent to infringe and the effect.

speaker: Amy Coney Barrett
text: So are you saying you'd amend your complaint?

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: Absolutely, Your Honor. We would  -- we very much want the opportunity to amend.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: That would normally be the course  under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and all I'm trying to say is I think the case for our opportunity to amend is even stronger here given that there -- you know, there's been a material change in the case since the Federal Circuit's opinion.

speaker: Michael R. Huston
text: We've uncovered all of this new evidence.

text: And so, again, the case has the same posture as all the cases cited on, I think, page 51 of our brief. A district court judge grants a motion to dismiss.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Thank you, Your Honor. I want to start by addressing this -- this point with no specifics that somehow new evidence came up in discovery that supports a claim for active inducement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Just to be clear, there is no such evidence, no evidence that  Hikma somehow intended its archived prelaunch litigation-related press releases to induce infringement or its online product catalogue to induce infringement.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Zero evidence.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The dismissal below also was with prejudice, and it was with prejudice because Amarin conceded to that judgment.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And so, if  -- if the Court were to remand, it -- it  -- the only thing left  -- or, if the Court were to reverse and remand, the only thing left would be a Rule 60 motion, and Amarin could file that if  -- if -- if they wish. I do want to address this argument that the conduct element turns on how a physician would understand vague and equivocal statements.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That  --that is not the standard when there's an obvious alternative explanation.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: Twombly and Iqbal make it very  clear, if there's an obvious alternative explanation, a complaint doesn't survive the  pleadings stage just because maybe some physician out there might possibly read an instruction to infringe into an equivocal or vague statement like generic version of Vascepa.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And there are obvious alternative explanations for all the accused statements in this case.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The -- the press releases that are  accused were all archived as of the launch. They concern litigation victories.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And  -- and  --and they  -- the only indication mentioned is Vascepa's non -infringing indication.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: At the time of launch  -- and this is in the record -- the November 2020 press  release, so this is when the product's first available, makes it clear the product is only accused  -- the --the product is only approved for the non -infringing indication and not approved for any other indication.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: And it has all the labeling information in the press release itself.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That  --there's no way that induces infringement. I do want to talk about the web page because I don't think my friend accurately characterized the web page.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The web page  refers to an AB rating for hypertriglyceridemia, which is a lot of jargon,  but the jargon is conceded and explained in the complaint and in the decision below, and it means therapeutically equivalent only as labeled to reduce high triglycerides.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That's  what it means.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The label is linked to the web page.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: So there is no plausible way to read that web page as somehow encouraging doctors to go off -label and -- and use the product for a patented method that has been carved out.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: That is not plausible.

speaker: Charles B. Klein
text: The obvious alternative explanation is the plain reading of  -- of the  -- of the web page. I see I'm out of time.
